Introduction and Pipeline Overview
sections.text:
The objective of this study is to analyze the scalability and performance characteristics of a real-world Large Language Model (LLM) data preprocessing pipeline implemented in PySpark. The pipeline, detailed in the code file a1 v1.0.py , processes raw web crawl data (WARC files) through a series of six stages to produce clean, tokenized training data.
The goal of this report is to provide a detailed analysis of the pipeline’s behavior under different resource configurations. We will evaluate its strong scaling performance, its weak scaling performance, and its sensitivity to executor memory allocations. All data presented in this report is derived from the figure table plotting.ipynb notebook.

subsections.title: Pipeline Stages
subsections.text:
The LLM preprocessing pipeline consists of six distinct stages, each performing a specific trans- formation on the data. The logic and resource consumption of each stage contribute uniquely to the overall scaling characteristics observed in the experiments.
• Step 1: WARC to Parquet Conversion (Ingestion & Parsing): The raw input data consists of .warc files stored on HDFS. This stage lists these files and processes them in parallel using a Spark RDD flatMap operation. For each record within a WARC file, it filters for response records containing HTML content and parses the headers and content. The output is a structured DataFrame, which is then written to HDFS in the efficient Parquet format, partitioned by the source filename. This stage is primarily I/O-bound and involves parsing unstructured data.
• Step 2: Domain Filtering: The pipeline ingests the Parquet data and filters out records originating from a predefined blacklist of domains. It loads a list of blacklisted domains from HDFS and broadcasts it to all executors for efficient lookups. The core of the logic involves extracting the host from the URL, generating all possible parent domains (e.g., sub.example.com - > example.com ), and performing a broadcast join against the blacklist to identify and remove unwanted records. This stage is CPU-bound for domain extraction and network/shuffle-bound for the join operation.
• Step 3: Text Extraction with Trafilatura: The raw HTML content from the filtered records is passed to the trafilatura library. This library performs complex parsing to extract clean, readable main text content, stripping away boilerplate, ads, and naviga- tion menus. This is a highly CPU-intensive operation, executed as a user-defined func- tion (UDF) over the DataFrame. The performance of this stage is highly dependent on the complexity of the HTML and is typically the computational bottleneck of the entire pipeline.
• Step 4: Language Identification (FastText): The extracted text is fed into a fasttext language identification model to detect its language. The model, a pre-trained binary file distributed to nodes via Spark’s file management, predicts the language for each document. Only documents classified as English with a probability above a threshold (de- fault 0.6) are retained. Like Step 3, this stage involves a UDF and is computationally expensive, but it is generally faster than the text extraction step. The fasttext model is loaded once per executor, which is a key optimization.
• Step 5: Deduplication: This stage employs two methods to remove duplicate content, as studied in the experiments:
– 5a. Near-Duplicate Deduplication (MinHash LSH): To remove near-duplicate
documents (e.g., articles that are very similar but not identical), the pipeline uses
Spark MLlib’s MinHashLSH . It converts text into character 5-grams, hashes them, and generates MinHash signatures. An LSH model is then used to find pairs of documents with a Jaccard distance less than or equal to 0.5. From each cluster of similar documents, only the longest one is kept. This process involves significant computation for feature extraction and a large, shuffle-heavy self-join to find similar pairs.
– 5b. Exact Deduplication (MD5): This simpler method calculates an MD5 hash
of the entire extracted text. Records with duplicate MD5 hashes are considered identical, and only one copy (the earliest by date) is retained. This is a lightweight operation compared to MinHash LSH, requiring minimal computation and shuffle.
• Step 6: Tokenization: The final stage converts the cleaned text into fixed-length token sequences suitable for LLM training. It tokenizes the text using a regex word-boundary pattern, maps each word to a token ID using a hashing function (bounded by a vocabulary size), and then either truncates or pads the sequence to a maximum length of 512 tokens. An attention mask is generated to distinguish real tokens from padding. This is a CPU- bound stage executed via a UDF.

sections.title: Experimental Setup
sections.text:
All experiments were conducted on a dedicated YARN cluster. The cluster configuration and experiment methodology are as follows:
• Cluster Hardware: 8 nodes, each with 72 vcores (hyper-threaded) and 128 GiB of RAM.
• YARN Queue: Jobs were submitted to a dedicated team queue ( root.ds256.team8 ) with a guaranteed capacity of 8.33% of the cluster, which could expand to a maximum of 25%.
• Spark Configuration (Baseline):
– Executor Memory Overhead: Set to 2GB unless overridden in the memory sen-
sitivity study.
– Metrics: spark.executor.processTreeMetrics.enabled and
spark.eventLog.logStageExecutorMetrics were enabled to capture detailed per- formance data, which was processed by scripts/extract metrics.py to produce the metrics in the final data.csv file.
• Data Sets: The input data consisted of six datasets of varying sizes, named small X , with the following sizes in GB:
– small 1 : 3.9 GB
– small 2 : 7.8 GB
– small 4 : 15.7 GB
– small 6 : 23.4 GB
– small 8 : 31.0 GB
– small 16 : 62.2 GB
• Experiment Methodology: Each configuration was run multiple times ( iterations=3 ) to account for runtime variability. A 10-second cool-down period was enforced between runs to allow for cluster cleanup. Key metrics such as stage times, total execution time, and deep JVM metrics (GC, shuffle, compute ratios) were captured for each run. More information about the metrics used is provided in the Appendix.

subsections.title: Parallel Efficiency
subsections.text:
Efficiency E = S ( N ) /N measures how effectively added cores are utilized. Table 1 and Figure 2 show a steep and continuous decline. The steepest drop (99% → 48%) occurs between 8 and 32 cores, after which the decline continues more gradually. Beyond 64 cores, each additional core delivers practically no improvement – hardware resources are effectively wasted.
The optimal operating region lies between 32 and 64 cores , where absolute execution time is meaningfully reduced (from 519s to 336s) while maintaining acceptable efficiency above 37%. The efficiency, which measures how effectively added cores are utilized, drops significantly from 63.9% at 16 cores to just 18.3% at 128 cores (Figure 2 ). This indicates that for this 7.8 GB dataset, the optimal resource allocation is around 64 cores. Beyond this point, the overhead of task scheduling, coordination, and diminishing returns from task parallelism outweigh the benefits of adding more cores.

A deeper look at the resource ratios (Table 3 , Figure 4a ) reveals the primary bottleneck. As the number of cores scales up, the ”Communication Ratio” increases dramatically from a negli- gible 0.51% at 8 cores to 8.55% at 128 cores. This is a classic symptom of Amdahl’s Law, where the serial portion of the workload (in this case, the need to shuffle data for operations like the LSH self-join) begins to dominate. The rising communication ratio directly explains efficiency loss: at 128 cores, 1 in 10 executor-seconds is spent on inter-node shuffle, not computation. Concurrently, the ”Compute Ratio” decreases.

The results in Table 5 and Figure 5a clearly show that using 4 cores per executor yields signif- icantly better performance than 2 cores. The execution time for the largest dataset (31 GB) is 1206 seconds with 4-core executors, compared to 2369 seconds with 2-core executors. The time per unit of data (Figure 5b ) shows a general upward trend, especially for the 2-core executor configuration, confirming that overhead increases with the scale of the job. The 4-core configuration, while faster, also shows a noticeable increase in execution time as data grows, particularly at the 32-core/15.7 GB point.

subsections.title: Resource Contention and Spill
subsections.text:
A key observation from the weak scaling experiment is the relationship between data size and memory spill. As shown in Figure 8a , the amount of memory spill increases almost linearly with the dataset size. With the fixed 8GB per executor, larger datasets force Spark to spill more intermediate data to disk, which is a major contributor to the increase in execution time. This effect is less pronounced for the 4-core executors, as they can process their larger share of data more efficiently within their memory space. The 2-cores/executor configuration maintains ≈ 98–99% compute ratio even as performance degrades – an artifact where disk spill I/O time is counted as compute, masking the true bottleneck. The 4-cores/executor configuration honestly shows compute declining to ≈ 90% and communication rising to ≈ 9% at 64 cores, mirroring the strong scaling pattern.
The 4-core executor configuration also shows a lower and more stable time per unit data (Fig- ure 5b ), suggesting it is a more efficient and scalable choice for this pipeline. The performance of the 2-core configuration degrades more rapidly, highlighting that for a compute-intensive pipeline, having more cores per executor is beneficial. memory spill grows from ≈ 4 GB to ≈ 32 GB for 2-cores/executor – an 8 × increase for 16 × data – confirming super-linear growth. The 4-cores/executor configuration is more moderate, reaching ≈ 23.5 GB at 64 cores. The crossover where 4-cores/executor is strictly better on all memory metrics occurs at ≈ 15–16 total cores.

caption.text: Figure 11: Memory sensitivity – execution time and spill vs. executor memory.
Figure 11a shows that execution time improves from 2 GB ( ≈ 1,550 s) to 6 GB ( ≈ 1,350 s), after which it increases to ≈ 2,080 s at 8 GB and degrades further at 10 GB.

Two mechanisms explain the counter-intuitive rise: (1) larger YARN containers take longer to schedule on the cluster; (2) larger Spark shuffle buffers increase total data written during sort-merge before spilling, paradoxically generating more intermediate work.
The widening error bars at higher memory values confirm non-deterministic YARN placement behaviour.
6–8 GB is the practical sweet spot beyond which additional memory hurts more than it helps.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text:
This scalability study provides a detailed performance analysis of an LLM data preprocessing pipeline. The key findings are:
1. Strong Scaling: The pipeline scales effectively up to 64 cores for a 7.8 GB dataset. Beyond this point, communication overhead from shuffle-intensive operations (like the domain filter join and deduplication) becomes the dominant bottleneck, limiting further speedup. Strong scaling achieves 2 . 97 × speedup (37% efficiency) at 64 cores before sat- urating completely due to a 67% serial fraction dominated by S5a’s MinHash shuffle overhead.
2. Weak Scaling: The pipeline handles increasing data sizes, but execution time does not remain constant. Configurations with 4 cores per executor significantly outperform those with 2 cores, demonstrating the benefit of more powerful executors for compute-intensive workloads. Memory spill increases linearly with data size, contributing to performance degradation. Weak scaling degrades 55% over 16 × data scale-up, with shuffle read time exploding to 3,450 s at 64 cores.
3. Memory Sensitivity: Allocating sufficient memory to executors is critical to minimize performance-degrading disk spill and GC overhead. For a 31 GB dataset with 16 two-core executors, 8 GB of memory per executor was found to be the optimal balance. Memory spill ( ≈ 11.7 GB average) is structurally driven by the LSH self-join and is completely insen- sitive to executor heap allocation – counter-intuitively, allocating more memory increases execution time.
4. Recommendations: For jobs similar to this pipeline, we recommend:
• The recommended production configuration is 4 cores/executor, 4–5 GB mem- ory, 8–16 executors for datasets under 32 GB. Scaling beyond that requires algo- rithmic redesign of S5a – the pipeline’s single greatest obstacle to production-scale deployment.
• Using executors with 4 cores, as they provide a better ratio of computational power to memory.
• Allocating memory such that intermediate data can be held in memory to avoid spill, with 8 GB per executor serving as a good baseline for similar data volumes.
• Recognizing that the pipeline’s scalability is limited by shuffle-heavy operations; fu- ture optimization efforts should focus on minimizing shuffle in stages like domain filtering and LSH-based deduplication.

Metric Definition
Executors Number of JVM processes launched to execute tasks. Each executor runs on a node in the cluster and man- ages resources for a set of tasks. Executors are launched at the beginning of a Spark application and run for its entire lifetime. Cores per Executor Number of CPU cores allocated to each executor.
